brief: TS Lombard argues 2026's US equity resilience, despite Middle East conflict, a hawkish Fed and surging bond yields, came down to earnings: corporate profits hit a record share of GDP, with tech (two-thirds of EPS growth) and energy (a third) the drivers, compressing PE multiples even as indices hit records. AI bulls compare this to the 1990s Greenspan productivity-boom puzzle, but TS Lombard finds no equivalent data discrepancy today. Instead it identifies two different puzzles: a widening wedge between sticky core inflation and falling unit labor costs, and a broken link between the collapsing wage share and rising r* estimates. Its own read resolves both hawkishly: immigration-constrained labor supply plus reaccelerating demand will push wages up and productivity down in 2027, reversing the current profit-margin-friendly 'sweet spot.' Combined with fading energy-price tailwinds and peaking hyperscaler AI capex (over 80% of AI revenue is still 'recycled capex'), these forces are expected to slow 2027 corporate earnings growth. Longer term, TS Lombard leans toward the bearish, commoditization view of AI token economics over Gavin Baker's Jevons-paradox bull case, and holds that AI is labor-augmenting rather than labor-replacing, so the corporate profit share is unlikely to rise structurally.

cards.anchor: the energy sector alone accounts for around a third of 2026 earnings growth

cards.claim: More than 80% of AI-related revenues are still coming from recycled hyperscaler capex rather than external demand.
cards.anchor: more than 80% of AI-related revenues are still just coming from “recycled capex”

cards.claim: Hyperscalers' capital gains on their AI equity stakes, booked as 'other income,' have been a positive contributor to 2026 tech earnings.
cards.anchor: the “other income” that the hyperscalers are booking as a result of the capital gains they are realizing

cards.claim: Based on consensus forecasts, year-on-year hyperscaler AI capital spending growth is currently hitting its peak.
cards.anchor: we are currently hitting the peak in terms of year-on-year hyperscaler spending

cards.claim: Harris Kupperman of Praetorian Capital argues the AI industry will become commoditized, causing a railway-mania or fiber-optics-style crash.
cards.anchor: the entire industry will end up being commoditized, leading to a railway mania- or fibreoptics-style crash

cards.claim: Gavin Baker of Atreides Management argues NVIDIA will retain US companies' edge by acting as 'trainer of last resort,' backstopping the AI ecosystem.
cards.anchor: US companies will retain their edge in the Gavin Baker scenario that happens because NVIDIA acts as “trainer of last resort”

cards.claim: TS Lombard leans toward the bearish, commoditization thesis for AI token economics over the Jevons-paradox bull case.
cards.anchor: We lean towards the more bearish thesis and the idea that AI will eventually be commoditized

cards.claim: US corporate profits as a share of nominal GDP have risen to their highest level since World War II.
cards.anchor: profits as a ratio of nominal GDP – to its highest levels since WW2

cards.claim: US national-accounts (NIPA) corporate earnings rose 25% year-on-year in 2026 Q2, led by tech and energy.
cards.anchor: Earnings jumped an impressive 25% in the year to 2026Q2, with tech and energy leading the way

cards.claim: The gap between sticky core inflation and falling unit labor costs is unusually wide and widening.
cards.anchor: the recent gap is unusually wide – and seems to be getting wider

cards.claim: Fed officials have been raising their r* estimates even as the US labor share of income has collapsed to historical lows.
cards.anchor: economists have been raising their estimates of r*, even as the labour share has collapsed to historical lows

cards.claim: TS Lombard forecasts that immigration-constrained labor supply plus rising labor demand will produce a cyclical revival in wages and slower productivity.
cards.anchor: stronger labour demand is likely to produce a cyclical revival in wages, alongside slower productivity

cards.claim: The US has become a net energy exporter, and the resulting trade boost has added to 2026 corporate profits.
cards.anchor: the US has become a net energy exporter

cards.claim: TS Lombard expects the 2026 earnings boost from high energy prices to reverse in 2027 if the Middle East conflict resolves and energy prices fall.
cards.anchor: energy prices slump in 2027, the 2026 boost from this sector of the economy will reverse

cards.claim: TS Lombard states there is no question that AI-related capital spending will eventually slow.
cards.anchor: there is no question that capital spending will eventually slow

cards.claim: TS Lombard forecasts that in 2027 the composition of US growth will shift back toward employment from productivity.
cards.anchor: 2027 will bring another big reversal in these dynamics, with the composition of US growth shifting again

cards.claim: Research cited by TS Lombard finds stock-based compensation mismeasurement could account for roughly $200bn of missing labor compensation, reversing about a third of the labor share's decline since the late 1970s.
cards.anchor: around $200bn of missing labour compensation, which would reverse one third of the fall in the labour share

cards.claim: Research cited by TS Lombard finds the US labor share would be about 1.5 percentage points higher without tax-code distortions that incentivize reporting wages as profit via S corporations.
cards.anchor: the labour share would probably be another 1.5%pts higher without this tax distortion

cards.claim: Adjusting the wage share for depreciation narrows its gap below the 1947-2001 average to about 8 percentage points, versus 9.5 points unadjusted.
cards.anchor: the net labour share is around 8%pts below its 1947 –2001 average

cards.claim: TS Lombard holds a long-standing view that AI is labor-augmenting rather than labor-replacing, implying the corporate profit share is unlikely to rise structurally.
cards.anchor: we are sticking to our long-held view that AI is labour-augmenting rather than labour-replacing

cards.claim: TS Lombard concludes that no Greenspan-style hidden productivity boom or data discrepancy exists in the US economy today.
cards.anchor: whether similar, Greenspan-style “data discrepancies” exist today – spoiler alert: they don’t!

cards.claim: Most companies are not using AI very intensively, with typical usage estimated at only around two hours per week.
cards.anchor: the vast majority of companies are not using this new technology very intensively (typically only around two hours per week)

cards.claim: TS Lombard, citing San Francisco Fed capacity-utilization-adjusted data, finds recent US productivity gains come from running the economy hot rather than from AI technology diffusion.
cards.anchor: all the recent improvement in US productivity has come from simply “running the economy hot”, not from the diffusion of a new technology
